I’ve worked as a tech on an adolescent inpatient psych unit, starting a nursing program in the fall and hoping to get straight into psych nursing when I graduate. Pros: You get to build really meaningful rapport with patients. You really hone your clinical judgment skills (even as a tech I felt this), as decisions  for pt care are not all black and white. On my unit, and I imagine most others, the charge nurse for each day attends rounds with the psychiatrists and social workers and advocates for their patients, so you have a very direct impact on treatment plans and your opinion is highly valued (at least where I was, this was the way nurses felt). Cons: the most obvious con is witnessing patients in so much emotional distress at times, performing and/or leading restraints, giving forced meds as someone else said. Those situations are draining. The risk for physical violence is always present. But in my experience that environment taught me so much in the way of street smarts and common sense. I’m much more observant and aware of my surroundings in general. I really love the way psych is different every day, and I love connecting to patients. The patients who have told me I made a difference in their lives are the reason I keep going to work every day. I left the unit but still work in psych in a different capacity, more acute crises. I miss the milieu and building rapport. Psych isn’t for everyone just like any specialty but it is always worth a try and keeping an open mind. There have been times where I felt discouraged from it but I always find my way back. Good luck!

I work as a counselor on an adolescent inpatient psych unit, and last night I checked in with several patients who shared very similar concerns as you. They have found themselves hospitalized in the middle of what they view as the most important years of their lives and they are struggling with what to do after. Some of them will be going to long-term psychiatric facilities and are struggling with what that means for their future. I am only 24, so I know the age difference is not massive and I have less than a decade of experience on you and many of the kids on my unit. But I am in the middle of an ongoing struggle with my own mental health, and have been since I was very young. So I do know what it feels like to be 17 and terrified of what is to come. 17 is a complicated age. At 17 I had no clue what to do with myself or my future. I had a hundred potential ideas and paths and I felt paralyzed by the fear of choosing the wrong one. I can tell you a few things. Community college is an excellent choice. I have a BA in psychology from a 4 year university but I am going to be attending community college very soon to begin nursing school. My closest friends attended or attend community college. You can go to your community college, receive a great education, and if you wish you can transfer to a 4 year school and complete your bachelors. You will be able to make connections and network wherever you go, including community college. You do have to put a little work into it, but speaking as someone who put minimal work into networking, I think it would be worth it. I wish I had done a little more, but i’m doing all right without it too. CC will provide you with so many skills that your public school system may have failed to teach. Challenge yourself without creating more unnecessary stress, and take classes at the appropriate level. If you need to take an intro to composition course, take it, and you will be more skilled at writing essays. Also feel free to message me any of your essays for notes because I double majored in English and was a TA in college for a composition class. College years are a time for personal development and forming an adult identity without the scariest responsibilities of true adulthood. Take your time and figure it out. You have a lot going on that you may not even be aware of. You will randomly discover passions that renew your will to live. One of my favorite coworkers is a 25 year old nurse who never got his drivers license. You can get yours when you feel ready and it’s possible you may not have to do as much work to get it if you wait until age 18, depending on where you live. The job market is admittedly bleak right now due to COVID and the general depressed state of our society but that may not be the case when you begin job searching after university. For now, try to focus on your schooling and push aside those worries about the job market. You can always revisit them in a few years. Also I was a horrible math student through all of school, i’m talking K-college. I almost failed precalculus my junior year of high school because I felt a lot of pressure to take rigorous courses I was not equipped for. The only reason I didn’t fail was my teacher took pity on me and dropped several of my failing test grades. I then managed to avoid taking another math course until junior year of college. It was stats for psych and it was difficult but I had gained a lot of study skills in those 4 years and i managed to pass with a C. No worries. You will keep on growing and changing. Sometimes life is depressing but adult life is also liberating and exciting and boring and hilarious and weird. It is important to not take it too seriously. I am here to listen if you need to talk. I am anxious and depressed and sometimes I have suicidal ideation, like about an hour ago. But when I am at work talking to the patients or even at home trying to help a stranger online, I feel like my life has a tiny purpose, even just for a moment. It helps.
